metadata.note: Curated subset for endpoint forensics — NOT the full ATT&CK matrix. Technique IDs are stable references; names and tactic assignments follow the ATT&CK snapshot above. Descriptions are HuntForge's own summaries, written for analysts. 'huntforge_sources' lists the (source, event_id) pairs whose parsed events can evidence the technique; an empty list means HuntForge cannot currently observe it (a documented coverage gap, not an omission).

techniques.description: PowerShell is built into Windows, trusted by administrators, and powerful enough to download payloads, reflectively load code, and bypass simple allowlists — which is exactly why attackers reach for it.
techniques.detection_notes: Encoded command lines and download patterns are the strongest tells; see HF-DET-ENCPSH and HF-DET-DLPSH.
techniques.name: PowerShell

techniques.description: cmd.exe is simple, present on every Windows host, and easy to invoke from scripts, macros, and other processes — a workhorse for both admins and intruders.
techniques.detection_notes: Watch for cmd.exe with unusual parents (Office, browsers) or spawning from writable directories.
techniques.name: Windows Command Shell

techniques.description: Windows Task Scheduler runs programs on triggers — logon, idle, a schedule. Malware abuses it for persistence and delayed execution; tasks whose actions live in user-writable paths deserve scrutiny.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-TASK (writable task action).
techniques.name: Scheduled Task/Job

techniques.description: Values under the Run and RunOnce keys execute at user logon — the most common Windows persistence mechanism. Legitimate installers use them too, so the target binary and execution evidence decide.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-RUNKEY — severity rises when the target binary is observed executing.
techniques.name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder

techniques.description: Services start at boot, often as SYSTEM. A service whose image lives outside protected directories can be both a persistence mechanism and a privilege-escalation path.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-SVC (service with user-writable image path).
techniques.name: Windows Service

techniques.description: Deleting or clearing event logs destroys forensic evidence. HuntForge cannot see what was deleted — but the absence of expected logs, or a 1102 record where one survives, is itself a signal.
techniques.detection_notes: Not currently parsed (needs Security log 1102). Documented coverage gap.
techniques.name: Clear Windows Event Logs

techniques.description: Removing tools, droppers, or logs after execution hides the tooling. Only file creation is parsed today, so deletions are inferred from timeline gaps, not observed directly.
techniques.detection_notes: Not currently parsed (needs Sysmon 23 FileDelete). Documented coverage gap.
techniques.name: File Deletion

techniques.description: Dumping the LSASS process memory yields credentials and hashes. The classic tell is a process opening LSASS with full access rights.
techniques.detection_notes: Not currently parsed (needs Sysmon 10 ProcessAccess targeting lsass.exe). Documented coverage gap.
techniques.name: LSASS Memory

techniques.description: RDP moves between hosts using valid credentials, blending with administrator activity. Logon type 10 in the Security log is the on-host evidence.
techniques.detection_notes: Correlate 4624 logons with the source host's own timeline; see HF-DET-ADMINHOST.
techniques.name: Remote Desktop Protocol

techniques.description: Listing files and directories to map the filesystem before acting. Weakly visible — usually just a command line like 'dir' or 'tree'.
techniques.detection_notes: Low-fidelity signal; useful only in sequence with other discovery commands.
techniques.name: File and Directory Discovery

techniques.description: Learning who owns the machine (whoami, quser) — a common first step after gaining access, to gauge the value of the foothold.
techniques.detection_notes: Low-fidelity alone; meaningful in a discovery cluster.
techniques.name: System Owner/User Discovery

techniques.description: Enumerating running processes (tasklist) to find security tooling, interesting targets, or competing malware.
techniques.detection_notes: Low-fidelity alone; meaningful in a discovery cluster.
techniques.name: Process Discovery

techniques.description: Reading network configuration (ipconfig, route print) to understand the environment — subnets, gateways, DNS — before moving.
techniques.detection_notes: Low-fidelity alone; meaningful in a discovery cluster.
techniques.name: System Network Configuration Discovery

techniques.description: Listing active connections (netstat) to find peers, existing sessions, and exfiltration paths.
techniques.detection_notes: Low-fidelity alone; meaningful in a discovery cluster.
techniques.name: System Network Connections Discovery

techniques.description: Enumerating network shares (net view, net share) to find the next hop for lateral movement.
techniques.detection_notes: Low-fidelity alone; meaningful in a discovery cluster.
techniques.name: Network Share Discovery

techniques.description: The user runs a malicious file — the classic maldoc/malware execution step. An Office application spawning a shell is the tell-tale shape; execution from a writable directory is another.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-OFFICE (Office ancestry) and HF-DET-TEMPEXEC (writable execution).
techniques.name: Malicious File

techniques.description: A targeted email attachment starts the intrusion chain. HuntForge sees the execution side (an Office app spawning a shell), not the delivery — the email itself is PhishScope's job.
techniques.detection_notes: Partial: execution ancestry only. Delivery evidence (the email) is out of scope for HuntForge.
techniques.name: Spearphishing Attachment

techniques.description: Files move into the victim environment — tools, payloads, second stages. PowerShell download cradles, bitsadmin, and certutil are the usual vehicles.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-DLPSH (PowerShell downloading remote content).
techniques.name: Ingress Tool Transfer

techniques.description: Data leaves over the existing command-and-control channel instead of a separate exfiltration path — harder to distinguish from normal C2 traffic.
techniques.detection_notes: Network telemetry shows the channel, not the data; exfiltration itself is inferred, never observed, from connection records alone.
techniques.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

techniques.description: Command and control over everyday protocols (HTTP/S, DNS) so the traffic blends with normal activity.
techniques.detection_notes: Connection records show the protocol and port, not the intent.
techniques.name: Application Layer Protocol

techniques.description: C2 on an unusual port dodges port-based detection. Worth pivoting on — the process, the destination, the surrounding timeline — but never proof on its own.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-RAREPORT (outbound connection to rare external port).
techniques.name: Non-Standard Port

techniques.description: Repeated password guessing against logon services. On the host it looks like a burst of failed logons — which is also what mistyped passwords look like, so context decides.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-BRUTE (5+ failed logons in 10 minutes). A burst followed by success is far more interesting.
techniques.name: Brute Force

techniques.description: Using legitimate credentials — stolen, guessed, or created — so the activity looks like normal administration. A privileged account appearing from a new source is the tripwire.
techniques.detection_notes: See HF-DET-ADMINHOST (privileged logon from first-seen host).
techniques.name: Valid Accounts
